The Security Council’s resolutions on Iran’s nuclear programme, including resolution 1929 (2010), were reinstated on 27 September 2025. In this regard, I would like to draw attention to the note issued on 28 September 2025 by the Secretary - General of the United Nations, taking note of the reinstatement of these resolutions. Paragraph 29 of resolution 1929 (2010) provides for the establishment, for an initial term of one year, of a Panel of Experts tasked with assisting the Committee established pursuant to resolution 1737 (2006). The reinstatement of resolution 1929 (2010) led to the reactivation of this mandate until 26 September this year. It is therefore legitimate and necessary for a draft resolution aimed at extending the mandate of this Panel to be submitted to the Council. France will therefore vote in favour of the provisional agenda.

In the light of the request made and the remarks made by members of the Security Council, I shall now put the provisional agenda to the vote.

As conflicts in the Middle East drag on and the process of achieving a political settlement of the Iranian nuclear issue remains deadlocked, the more turbulent the situation becomes, the more the Security Council must demonstrate leadership and act responsibly,

Draft resolution S/2026/740, submitted to the Council today, had a simple purpose — to renew the mandate of the independent Panel of Experts of the Committee established pursuant to resolution 1737 (2006) tasked with assisting said Committee and monitoring the implementation of resolutions concerning Iran’s nuclear programme.

France voted in favour of this text because it supports the full implementation of those resolutions, which were reinstated a year ago in accordance with the procedures set out in resolution 2231 (2015), a move prompted by Iran’s serious and repeated breaches of its commitments under the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. This decision was not taken unexpectedly, but following months of fruitless negotiations between Iran and the E3 —France, Germany and the United Kingdom — notably in Geneva, which demonstrated Iran’s stubborn refusal to comply with its non-proliferation obligations.

We regret that the veto by two Council members has prevented the renewal of this Panel’s mandate. We also regret that a few days ago those same two Council members prevented the recruitment of the experts proposed by the Secretariat to form this Panel. The veto deprives the 1737 Committee and the Council of an indispensable tool for ensuring the proper implementation of their decisions. It deprives the entire international community of a reliable and impartial source of information on a critical issue of international peace and security. And, just like the veto cast two years ago against the renewal of the panel on North Korea, this veto undermines the international non-proliferation regime, which is a cornerstone of our collective security. The role of this Panel of Experts would have been all the more important at a time when Iran’s violations of its international obligations, and specifically of the Council’s resolutions, poses serious threats to international peace and security.

The state of Iran’s nuclear programme remains a major cause for concern, as Iran continues to obstruct any resumption of cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). In this regard, we take note of the recent decision by the IAEA Board of Governors to refer to the Security Council the issue of Iran’s non - compliance with its comprehensive safeguards agreement under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. Iran’s ballistic missile programme also continues to threaten regional stability, as demonstrated by the indiscriminate strikes carried out in recent months against the Gulf States. It should be recalled that resolution 1929 (2010) prohibits Iran from carrying out activities related to ballistic missiles capable of delivering nuclear weapons.
